import importlib.util
for m in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES', len(r.pages))
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1}.txt').write_text(text)
 print(f'PAGE {i+1}: {len(text)} chars; box={p.mediabox}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+p.read_text() for i,p in enumerate(sorted(Path('tmp/pdfs').glob('page-*.txt'), key=lambda p:int(p.stem.split('-')[1])))))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem: locally repairing misalignment where a seam crosses problematic structures. The selective patch-repair approach is simple, requires no training, and integrates with existing seam-cutting pipelines.

Table I reports consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods and 79 image pairs from three datasets. For example, Baseline+LPAM improves SEAGULL seam SSIM from 0.638 to 0.696 and reduces RMSE from 0.106 to 0.096. The visual examples corroborate useful local repairs.
The pipeline diagrams, pseudocode, reported parameter settings, and code/data link support understanding and reproducibility. Established methods and benchmark datasets are generally attributed.

The discussion candidly identifies failure cases involving widespread seam errors and small patches with substantial displacement. These examples help establish the method’s intended operating conditions.
weaknesses: The contribution beyond existing seam-guided alignment is insufficiently established. Section II characterizes prior methods as operating on settled alignments, although its own descriptions of SEAGULL [25] and dense-matching-based stitching [21] involve adapting the warp. Neither receives a dataset-wide quantitative comparison; the comparison with Parallax and SEAGULL is limited to one illustrated scene. The distinctive benefit of selective patch repair therefore remains uncertain.

The central warp definition is ambiguous. Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Equation (5) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized spatial position. The intended weighting of the displacement is not explicitly specified. Moreover, the sigmoid does not reach exactly zero or one at the boundaries, and the horizontal-coordinate description does not explain continuity around an entire rectangular patch. Boundary label constraints ensure compatible seam labels but do not themselves guarantee continuous image geometry.

The experiments primarily compare complete LPAM against its absence. Figure 3 provides a useful single-example illustration, but there are no quantitative ablations establishing the effects of patch selection, flow modification, or constrained seam merging, nor sensitivity analyses for k, beta, and patch extent. These omissions matter because the disclosed failures directly depend on selection and patch size.

The evaluation supports improved local image agreement more strongly than improved overall perceptual quality. SSIM also drives patch selection, while the reported agreement metrics do not directly assess geometric distortion or content preservation. Selected visual examples offer partial corroboration, but dataset-wide failure and degradation rates are absent. In particular, the claim that false-positive selections do not yield inferior results is not established.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. Table III reports approximately 6–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, which is substantial relative to several underlying seam cutters. Alignment is excluded, image resolutions are unspecified, and no end-to-end runtime comparison with seam-driven alternatives establishes a favorable quality–computation tradeoff.
